OCCASION AND ORIGIN OF THIS WORK.—The deacon Quodvultdeo had been insisting to Saint Augustine on the need for a manual on heresies, begging him since the year 427 to write a compendium in which he would collect everything the known heresies teach!

Saint Augustine excuses himself by referring him to the Panarion, by Saint Epiphanius, which can be found and translated in Carthage, because it is an important work 2. Quodvultdeo responds by insisting that he did not expect to find there either the refutation of all the heresies or the adequate translation. But one of these letters is lost with Quodvultdeo's sending to Saint Augustine of the translation of Saint Epiphanius's work. And now Quodvultdeo insists with greater urgency that Saint Augustine write a more practical work on heresies than that of Saint Epiphanius.

Saint Augustine does not respond to this urgency of Quodvultdeo with another new letter. But he begins to work on this assignment, after he has finished his two books of the Revisions and also responded to the five books of Juliano?

When Saint Augustine finishes the first part of this work, with the prologue he gives a practical response to Quodwultdeo, sending him that first part of the written work, which he titles De Haeresibus (The Heresies).

TIME AND PLACE.—Therefore, Saint Augustine wrote the work The Heresies between the years 428-429. The place where he wrote it is Hippo, because it is to that address where Quodvultdeo sends his letters, and Saint Augustine answers him with the bearer also from Hippo.

ARIANS, from Arius, are well known for that error with which they deny that the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit are of one and the same nature and substance or, to put it more clearly, esence, which in Greek is called ousia, but that the Son is a creature, but also that the Spirit is a creature of the creature, that is, they want it to be created by the Son himself. On the other hand, they are much less known in their opinion that Christ received the flesh alone without the soul. And I can't find anyone who has refuted them on this point. And this is true. Epifanio did not keep it quiet either, and I have verified it with absolute certainty through some of his writings and conversations. We know that they also rebaptize Catholics; If they do the same to non-Catholics, I don't know (De Hacresibus, 1.49).

This work of Saint Augustine, Reply to the adversary of the law and the prophets, in two books, is a work of maturity and study. Important for the defense it makes of the Holy Scripture and for the clarification of many problems. At the same time, it is testimony to the sagacity and theological speculative sense that Saint Augustine shows he has on the Manichean problem, which he had already dealt with in other works, and on the complex Gnostic controversy. All of which is now raised again by the adversary of the law and the prophets with their erroneous interpretations. On the other hand, it has been a work very little studied in depth by specialists! and which, however, can bring many surprises, both in its style and in its content, which are not at all easy to understand and much less to simplify.

Occasion of this work by Saint Augustine. —He says it in the first lines of the work (1,1) and in the Revisions (2,58): A heretical book that was for sale and was read publicly in the Maritime Square of Carthage was bought by some brothers, and they sent it to Saint Augustine so that he could give a response as soon as possible, even briefly.

According to this, Saint Augustine had not been aware of this teaching, despite his bibliographical activity as a student or frequent visitor to Carthage. On the other hand, does the freedom with which it was taught publicly appear, despite the prohibition of the Codex Theodosianus? to every sect or heresy, and that for this reason the adversary posed as a Christian (1,3). But since Christ must be accepted completely as the true and supreme God (2,36), and it is not enough to pretend to be so as every heretic wants? Because any Christian heresy also has something against Christ (1,3), Saint Augustine answers him and refutes him in detail so that the simple who hear him are not deceived (1,1; Retractationes 2,58).

Author and title of the pamphlet. —Saint Augustine receives this book, whose author is an anonymous heretic. It is also an anonymous pamphlet, which Saint Augustine is not sure into which sect or heresy he classified.

The genius of Saint Augustine always took into account the importance of Judaism and its mysterious presence in the development of the City of God. He refers to it in his works in many ways. But this Treatise against the Jews is the only work of Saint Augustine that is addressed directly to them. And studied impartially, one sees in it the depth of the genius that values ​​Judaism in all its magnitude, and that discovers, with Isaiah and Saint Paul, above all the truth of the mystery of the people of Israel realized in Christianity and in the Church.
As a second-hand work, it presents some difficulties that must be resolved to better assess its content and purpose.
The difficulties are, above all, two: the title and the time.

Title. —The title is not uniform in the manuscripts that have preserved it.' This title, in all the manuscripts, with the pre: position adversus or contra (with a sense of opposition, confrontation or controversy, etc.), is completely unfair, because it does not correspond to its content, which is not polemical, but pastoral, nor does it go against the Jews, but rather in their favor as a chosen people, permanently called with a divine promise to conversion. If he sometimes uses his masterful command of rhetoric with some invective, he does so to break stubbornness and displays his pastoral zeal in order to get the Jews, at least some, to convert; and at the same time, to vigorously defend the faithful from their entanglements and proselytism. That is why he gives everyone the following instruction: Let us preach this with charity toward them (n. 15). Therefore, rather than Tractatus adversus ludaeos it should be titled Tractatus ad ludaeos or pro ludacis.
